summary: This unit teaches you to lead across a whole public organisation, not just your own team. You will learn to build a vision, mission and values that staff believe, shape a healthy culture, lead by example and ethically, align every unit with the corporate plan, work across silos and influence without authority, communicate and empower, choose a leadership approach, lead change and crises, develop future leaders and judge how well the organisation is being led.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It prepares you to **provide leadership across the organisation**: to guide an agency, ministry department, municipal corporation or school so that people in every unit understand where it is going, trust its leaders and pull in the same direction.

**Management** is about planning, organising and controlling work so that things are done properly. **Leadership** is about setting direction, inspiring people and bringing about change. Senior public servants need both. At this level you lead people you may rarely meet, through managers you do not directly supervise, and in a setting where Ministers, boards, unions, the media and the public all watch.
**Who it is for:** directors, senior managers, heads of departments and officers preparing for those roles.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Create and share a vision, mission and values
Say where the organisation is going, what it does, and how people will behave, in words staff believe.
Shape the culture and lead by example
Match what you say with what you do; build trust, learning and safety to speak up.
Lead ethically
Declare interests, resist improper pressure, stay politically neutral and promote integrity.
Align the organisation
Link every unit's plan to the corporate plan and measure results.
Work across units and influence others
Break down silos; win support from people you do not manage.
Communicate and empower
Reach everyone, listen upward, delegate real authority and share leadership.
Lead change and crises
Use a change model, bring people along, and give honest updates in a crisis.
Develop leaders and review leadership
Plan succession, coach and stretch people, and check results, surveys and feedback.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with short sums on targets met and response rates.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms) and longer answers.
**Group practical tasks**: writing a vision, values and leadership charter for a made-up agency, and leading a cross-department crisis response meeting and briefing all staff.

blocks.note: Most questions give a situation and ask what a senior leader should do. The best answer is usually open, consistent with the values, aimed at the organisation's purpose, and gives people the facts and a voice.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Term
What it is
Example (a municipal corporation)
rows: **Vision**
A short statement of the **future** the organisation is working towards
'Clean, safe and thriving communities in every part of the parish.'
**Mission**
What it does, for whom and how, **now**
'We deliver reliable local services to residents and businesses, fairly and efficiently.'
**Values**
The principles that guide how people behave
Integrity, service, respect, accountability, teamwork
**Strategic objectives**
The main results to achieve in the plan period
Cut waste-collection complaints by half in three years

blocks.p: The **vision** points ahead; the **mission** describes the present purpose. A vision statement is not a list of services or a slogan for a poster. A good one is short, clear, inspiring and believable, and it tells staff which direction is 'forward'.

blocks.h: Building and embedding a shared vision

flow: Listen: ask staff and users what the organisation is for and what is not working
Draft the vision and values with representatives from every unit and level
Test the draft with staff, the board and key stakeholders, and revise it
Launch it in person, in every office, explaining why it matters and inviting questions
Link it to plans, targets, recruitment, induction, appraisal and recognition
Show it in action: leaders visibly make decisions by it
Review it each year and measure whether it is felt

blocks.p: When the CEO wants staff in every parish office to understand a new vision, she should **explain it in person, say why it matters, and invite questions**, not email a poster and move on. A merged agency, with staff from two former bodies, needs to build the vision **with** both groups so that neither feels absorbed.
A value written on a wall is only words. Make each value **observable** by describing two or three behaviours that staff and leaders will show.

head: Value
What staff and leaders will do
What they will not do
rows: Integrity
Declare interests, tell the truth, own mistakes
Hide errors, bend the rules for friends
Service
Answer the public promptly and politely; fix the cause of complaints
Treat the public as an interruption
Respect
Listen, give credit, challenge ideas not people
Shout, humiliate, ignore
Accountability
Say who is responsible; report on results
Blame others; hide behind the process

blocks.p: If a ministry's values hang on the walls but managers ignore rude treatment of the public, staff will see the values as **words that do not matter**. The gap between stated values and actual behaviour does more harm than having no values at all.

blocks.note: Public service values in Jamaica include integrity, accountability, impartiality and service to the public. Link your agency's values to the standards in the public service code and the code of conduct your instructor gives you.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Organisational culture** is the shared beliefs, values and habits that shape how work is done. It is 'the way we do things here', and it shows in what people do when no one is watching. It is built by what leaders **pay attention to, reward, tolerate and do**.

head: Sign of a healthy learning culture
Sign of an unhealthy culture
rows: Staff can raise problems and lessons are shared
People hide mistakes and blame others
Decisions are made at the right level
Nothing moves without one person's signature
Leaders say 'I was wrong'
Leaders defend every decision
Questions and ideas are welcome from any level
Junior staff say nothing in meetings
Mistakes are studied for what they teach
Mistakes are punished, so they are concealed

blocks.p: Staff at a statutory body say, 'Here, nobody takes a decision without the director's signature.' The new director wants faster service. She should **set clear limits for decisions at each level and back staff who use them**. A decision-rights chart (who may decide what, up to what amount or risk) combined with visible support when a staff member makes a reasonable decision is more effective than a speech.

**Psychological safety** is a workplace where staff feel safe to speak up, ask questions and admit mistakes without being embarrassed or punished. It matters because the people closest to the work often see problems first. When junior officers rarely point out errors in senior managers' plans, leaders should **welcome challenge, thank those who raise issues and act on them**. If the first person to raise a problem is punished, no one will raise the next one.

ul: **Effects:** errors are hidden and grow; decisions are delayed because nobody wants to be wrong; good people leave; the public gets slower, poorer service.

**Cure:** treat a mistake as information. Ask 'what happened and what do we change?' before 'who did it?'. Separate honest mistakes from wilful wrongdoing. Recognise those who report problems early. Leaders talk openly about their own errors.

blocks.p: People watch what leaders do, not what they say. A CEO who orders a 20% cut in travel and then books a luxury trip herself destroys her own message: managers will **doubt her commitment and take the cut less seriously**. The behaviours that build trust across a large public body are **doing what you say you will do, and explaining your decisions**.

ul: Follow the rules you set for others (leave, travel, procurement, timekeeping).
Be seen where the work happens: visit the parish offices, the counters and the depots.
Admit and correct your own mistakes in public.
Give credit to others and share success.
Treat everyone, from the security guard to the board chair, with the same respect.
Own a mistake openly and explain how it will be fixed: this shows accountability more clearly than any slogan.

sections.title: Ethical leadership and the public-service setting

blocks.h: Why ethics matter more in public service

blocks.p: A public body spends **public money** and uses **public powers**. Citizens cannot choose another supplier. They need confidence that decisions are made fairly and that officials serve the public interest. One scandal can damage trust in the whole organisation.

A senior manager on a tender panel whose brother's company has bid must **declare the interest and step back** from the panel. Whenever your personal, family or financial interests could affect, or seem to affect, an official decision, declare, record it and take no part. A **conflict of interest** is a situation in which your personal interests could affect your official decisions.

Senior public servants are **politically neutral**. They serve any lawfully elected government fairly and give honest, evidence-based advice. This lets them keep the trust of the public and of every government. Neutrality is not silence or obedience to anything: you give frank advice, then carry out lawful decisions.

head: Pressure
The right response
rows: A Minister's adviser asks you to delay publishing a critical report
Explain that publication follows the law and the set procedure, offer to brief the Minister fully, record the request and tell your superior
A politician's supporter asks you to hurry their application
Explain that all applications follow the same process; do not give one person an advantage
A new Minister arrives after an election
Brief him or her frankly and impartially, keep your records, and serve the new government's lawful policy
A friend asks for inside information
Decline; confidential information belongs to the organisation

ul: Adopt and explain a **code of conduct**; train every new employee.
Keep a **register of interests** and a **gifts register**.
Make it safe to **report wrongdoing**, and protect those who do.
Follow procurement and financial rules strictly, and keep audit trails.
**Act on audit findings**: accept them, agree actions, name owners and dates, and track them to completion.
Apply the rules **equally**, including to senior people.

blocks.note: When an internal audit finds weak controls across several units, the CEO accepts the findings, agrees actions and tracks them to completion. Defending the units or delaying the report weakens trust.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Strategic alignment and working across units

blocks.h: The corporate plan and the cascade

blocks.p: A public body's **corporate plan** (also called a strategic plan or corporate strategy, normally covering three to five years) sets out its goals and priorities. Each year, an **operational (annual) plan** turns it into targets. Each unit then writes a **unit work plan**, and each person's **work plan and appraisal** links to it. This is called **alignment** or the 'golden thread'.

flow: Monthly and quarterly reports back up the line

blocks.p: **Example.** The corporate plan aims to cut the time for business registration. A supporting unit plan is: 'The registry unit will move all forms online by March and reduce average processing time to five days'. A plan that has nothing to do with the registration time, however good in itself, is not aligned.
Senior leaders ensure each unit's work plan links to the corporate plan so that **all units pull the same way towards shared goals**, and no resources are wasted on activities nobody asked for.

head: Measure
How to work it
Worked example
rows: Targets met
Met ÷ total × 100
22 of 40 targets met: 22 ÷ 40 × 100 = 55%
Survey response rate
Replies ÷ staff invited × 100
375 of 500 staff replied: 75%
Change in percentage points
New % - old %
From 52% to 68% = 16 points
Cost per participant
Total cost ÷ number

blocks.p: To stop a corporate plan sitting on a shelf, **review progress openly each quarter and adjust actions**. Publish a simple scorecard, ask unit heads to explain red and amber results, and recognise those who deliver.

blocks.h: Working across units and breaking silos

blocks.p: A **silo** is a unit that works alone and shares little with other units. Silos cause delays, duplication, contradictory messages to the public and blame between units. For example, if the licensing and inspection units each blame the other for long delays, the director should **bring both teams together to map the whole process and fix it jointly**, using the customer's journey as the common view, not the units' own boundaries.

head: Arrangement
What it does
rows: Cross-unit project team
Brings people from several units to solve one problem
Joint steering group
Senior officers from each unit or agency, with shared goals, agreed roles and shared targets
Shared data and systems
One record for the customer, not several
Shared targets and recognition
Units are rewarded for joint results, not only their own
Job rotation and joint training
People understand each other's work

blocks.p: When several ministries deliver a joint programme, for example on youth employment, the best arrangement is a **joint steering group with shared goals and clear roles**.

Senior leaders often need support from colleagues over whom they have no line authority. The most effective approach is to **learn each person's concerns and show how the proposal helps their unit**, rather than to order or to rely on rank.

ul: **Listen first.** Ask what each director needs and fears.
**Find common ground** and a shared benefit.
**Use evidence** such as data, user complaints and costs.
**Build a coalition**: win a few respected supporters early.
**Offer something**: resources, recognition or help with their problem.
**Keep promises**: reliability builds the trust that influence needs.

blocks.p: A **network of relationships** across the organisation helps a senior leader gain support and information when it is needed, because people share news and give help to those they trust.

A **stakeholder** is any person or group affected by, or able to influence, the organisation's work. A **stakeholder map** shows who is affected or has influence, and how to engage them (inform, consult, involve or partner).

ul: In a **ministry**, the **Permanent Secretary** is the administrative head and the **accounting officer**, who answers for the use of funds.
In a **statutory body**, the **board** sets direction, holds the CEO to account and oversees risk; the CEO leads management.
Before a decision such as **closing or merging offices**, consult **staff, their unions or associations, local users and community leaders** before deciding.
Plan a different approach for each group: staff need early notice and honesty; users need alternatives; the board and Minister need briefings.

blocks.note: Where a ministry, agency or municipal corporation is affected by a decision, remember to keep staff associations and unions informed under the employment law and the public service rules.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: When 900 staff in 14 parish offices must hear about a major change on the same day, the best approach is a single **all-staff briefing** (for example a video call, with recording) so everyone hears the same message, followed by **managers briefing their teams the same day**, and a written summary and a place for questions.

head: Need
Good practice
rows: Everyone hears the same thing
A single all-staff message from the top; then local briefings
Messages that fit each office
Managers add what it means locally
Reach staff without email
Notice boards, supervisors' briefings, text messages, posters
Hear from staff
Question time, suggestion boxes, surveys, walkabouts, an open-door hour

blocks.p: Communication must also go **upward**. Leaders who only broadcast do not learn what is really happening. Create ways for staff to send ideas and concerns up the line, and **respond** so they know they have been heard.

When rumours of job cuts spread and **no decision has been made**, the CEO should **tell staff what is and is not known, and when they will hear more**. Silence feeds rumours. Do not promise what you cannot guarantee.

**Empowerment** means giving people clear goals, the **authority** to act and the support to succeed. To make managers take more initiative: set clear goals, give clear decision rights, support their decisions (even if you would have chosen differently) and learn from errors without blame.
**Distributed leadership** is leadership shared among people at many levels, not just the top. A good leader develops leaders throughout the organisation.

head: Level of delegation
What the manager can do
rows: Look into it and report; I will decide
Recommend a course of action; I will decide
Decide and tell me before acting
Decide, act and tell me afterwards
Decide and act; report only by exception

blocks.p: For a major decision, such as moving a service online, **gather evidence, consult users and staff, weigh the risks and options, then decide**. After the decision, explain the reasons to staff, including those who disagree, **so they understand it** even if they would have chosen differently. Understanding is what turns compliance into support.

head: Approach
Main idea
When it helps
rows: **Transformational**
Inspires people with a vision, develops them and encourages new ideas; leaders show the way
Change, merging cultures, building commitment
**Transactional**
Sets clear tasks, rewards and corrections; focuses on rules, targets and performance
Routine services, compliance, clear standards
**Servant**
The leader puts the needs of staff and the public first and sees her role as helping others succeed
Building trust and teams in service organisations
**Adaptive**
Helps people face **new challenges that have no ready answer**; asks questions, experiments and learns
Complex problems without a known solution, such as a changing climate or new technology
**Situational**
Changes style (directing, coaching, supporting, delegating) to suit the person and task
A mixed team with different skill and confidence

blocks.p: A senior leader in a public body usually needs **both** transformational and transactional approaches: transactional to keep services running to standard, transformational to move the organisation forward.

ol: **Create a sense of urgency**: show why change cannot wait.
**Build a guiding coalition**: a team with the influence and trust to lead it.
**Form a strategic vision**: say where you are going.
**Enlist a volunteer army**: communicate the vision widely and invite people to take part.
**Remove barriers**: change rules, systems and structures that block progress, and empower action.
**Sustain acceleration**: do not declare victory too early; build on the wins.
**Institute change**: anchor the new ways in the culture, procedures and appraisal.

blocks.p: The **first step** is to create a sense of urgency.

blocks.h: Keeping staff with you in a change

blocks.p: When a public body moves to digital records and long-serving staff are anxious, leaders keep their support by **involving them early, training them well and listening to concerns**. Reasons for resistance include fear of lost skills, status or jobs, extra work, loss of control and past failures. Answer fear with information and support, not with orders.

flow: Check that all staff are safe and set up an emergency team
Assess what is damaged or stopped; protect key services
Decide priorities and who does what, with a log of decisions and owners
Communicate early and often with staff, the public and the Minister
Keep going with a clear command line and regular updates
Recover, then review what was learned

ul: After a hurricane damages several parish offices, the first priority is **people**: check that all staff are safe, and set up the emergency team.
Give **frequent, honest updates even when not everything is known**: trust is kept and rumours do not fill the gap.
Say when the next update will come, and keep to it.
Delegate: the leader cannot do everything. Use the people director, operations director and communications director.
Record every decision, with an owner and a time.

sections.title: Developing leaders, governance and reviewing leadership

blocks.p: When several directors are due to retire within three years, the senior team should **identify and develop managers who could take on those roles** now, not wait until the posts fall vacant. Succession planning protects the organisation from losing knowledge and leadership overnight.

head: Method
What it does
rows: Coaching
One-to-one help to reflect and improve
Mentoring
Guidance from a more experienced person
Stretch assignments
A task slightly beyond the person's present level, with support
Learning sets
Small groups of managers solve real problems together
360-degree feedback
Views from boss, peers and staff on the person's leadership
Courses and reading
Knowledge and models

blocks.p: A programme of **coaching, stretch assignments, learning sets and feedback** is more likely to build strong leaders than a single course.

**Judging a programme.** Define measures beforehand: completion (12 of 15 managers is 80%), cost per participant (J$3,000,000 ÷ 15 = J$200,000), and **results** such as the share of staff who say their manager gives useful feedback (52% before, 68% after: a rise of 16 percentage points). Gather feedback from participants and from their teams.

blocks.h: Governance: the board and the CEO

blocks.p: In a statutory body, the board sets direction, **holds the CEO to account** and oversees risk. The CEO leads management and the board does not run daily work. A leader supports a healthy relationship: honest reporting, no surprises, clear roles and respect for the board's decisions.
A senior leadership team judges how well it is leading by using **results data, staff surveys and stakeholder feedback, and by acting on them**.

head: Source
What it tells you
rows: Performance against the corporate plan
Whether the organisation is getting results
Staff engagement survey
How staff feel; check the response rate (420 of 600 is 70%)
Customer and stakeholder feedback
How the public and partners see the service
Audit, risk and complaint reports
Where controls and service are weak
360-degree feedback
How leaders' behaviour is experienced
Exit interviews and turnover
Why people leave

blocks.p: Review the results openly, tell staff what you found, and act. A survey that is never followed by action teaches staff that it is not worth answering.

blocks.note: A good leader asks, 'What would staff and the public say about how we lead?' and then asks them.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: tell a vision from a mission, and describe how to build and embed them.
turn values into observable behaviours.
describe organisational culture, and recognise a healthy and an unhealthy one.
explain psychological safety and how to build it.
show how leaders build trust by their own example.
handle conflicts of interest and resist improper political pressure while staying neutral.
promote integrity, including acting on audit findings.
link unit plans to the corporate plan and work out percentages of targets met.
break down silos and use cross-unit groups.
influence people over whom I have no authority.
communicate to all staff at once and open channels upward.
empower others and explain distributed leadership.
describe transformational, transactional, servant, adaptive and situational leadership.
list Kotter's eight steps and lead a change with staff on board.
lead through a crisis, develop future leaders and review how well the organisation is led.

terms: Vision
A short statement of the future an organisation is working towards.
Mission
A statement of what an organisation does, for whom and how, now.
Values
The principles that guide behaviour in an organisation.
Organisational culture
The shared beliefs, values and habits that shape how work is done.
Psychological safety
A workplace where staff feel safe to speak up, ask questions and admit mistakes.
Conflict of interest
A situation where personal interests could affect official decisions.
Political neutrality
Serving any lawful government fairly and impartially.
Corporate plan
A public body's main plan, usually three to five years, setting goals and priorities.
Alignment
Linking each unit's plan and each person's work to the corporate plan.
Silo
A unit that works alone and shares little with the rest of the organisation.
Stakeholder
A person or group affected by, or able to influence, the organisation's work.
Accounting officer
The head of a ministry (the Permanent Secretary) who answers for its use of funds.
Distributed leadership
Leadership shared among people at many levels.
Servant leadership
Leadership that puts serving staff and the public first.

Leadership that inspires people with a vision and develops them.
Adaptive leadership
Helping people face new challenges that have no ready answer.
Kotter's eight steps

An open meeting where senior leaders brief all staff and take their questions.
Succession planning
Preparing people now to fill senior posts in future.

c1.title: A blame culture at a water agency
c1.text: Mr Everard Blake is the new Director General of a rural water agency with 300 staff in 12 offices. In his first month he learns that an engineer hid a delayed pipeline repair for two weeks because 'the last person who reported a delay was transferred'. Staff say that nothing is done without the director's signature, even for small purchases. The agency's values, 'integrity, service and teamwork', are printed on every wall.

c2.title: The corporate plan at a registry
c2.text: A registry's corporate plan for three years aims to halve complaint response times. After the first year, it met 22 of its 40 annual targets. A staff engagement survey was sent to 500 staff and 375 replied. Of those who replied, 60% said they knew what the plan was trying to achieve. The CEO, Mrs Carol Reid, has the plan on her shelf and discusses it once a year with the board.

c3.title: Divisions that do not talk to each other
c3.text: A ministry of agriculture has an extension division that advises farmers and a marketing division that helps them sell. Farmers receive conflicting advice, and each division blames the other when produce is wasted. Mrs Janet Francis, a director in the ministry, wants both divisions and the planning unit to share one farmer database. She has no authority over the other directors.

c4.title: Moving payroll to a shared centre
c4.text: A statutory body with 600 staff in 10 offices decides to move payroll processing from each office to a central unit within a year. Rumours say that 40 payroll clerks will lose their jobs, though no decision on staffing has been made. The CEO, Mr Neville Gray, wants everyone to hear the news on the same day and wants managers to take responsibility for their teams.

c5.title: Pressure after a change of government
c5.text: After a general election, a new Minister's adviser asks Dr Sandra Morgan, a permanent secretary, to delay publication of an audit report that criticises a programme run by the previous administration. A few days later, Dr Morgan learns that one of her directors has accepted a free weekend at a resort from a firm bidding for a ministry contract.

c6.title: A leadership programme for middle managers
c6.text: A ministry spent J$3,000,000 on a one-year development programme for 15 middle managers. It included coaching, stretch assignments and feedback from teams. Twelve managers completed it. Before the programme, 52% of staff in their units said their manager gave them useful feedback. A year later, the figure was 68%.

questions.q: Staff say that mistakes are punished and that a delay was hidden. What is the most useful first step for Mr Blake?
o: Treat the delay as information and welcome staff who report early
Call a meeting to find and discipline the engineer who hid the delay
Order managers to send him a daily list of errors by their staff
Tell staff that mistakes will not be tolerated under his leadership
questions.why: Hiding a problem is a sign that staff fear blame. Treating a mistake as information and rewarding early reporting builds the safety needed for people to speak up.

questions.q: Staff say nothing is decided without the director's signature. What should he do to speed up service?
o: Sign everything faster and add a second signature for large purchases
Tell staff to make decisions as they see fit, without limits
Move all purchasing to the head office so decisions are made in one place
Set clear decision limits by level and back staff who use them
questions.why: Clear decision rights, with backing for those who use them, spread authority and speed up service while keeping control through limits.

questions.q: The values on the walls are 'integrity, service and teamwork', but staff behaviour has not changed. What is the best way to make them real?
o: Put larger posters in every office and repeat the words at each meeting
Ask staff to memorise the values and recite them at the annual meeting
Describe each value as behaviours that staff will show, and use it in appraisal
Replace the values with new words that the board likes better this year
questions.why: Values change what people do when they become observable behaviours that leaders model and that count in hiring, recognition and appraisal.

questions.q: Which action by Mr Blake would do the most to build trust?
o: Promising in a speech that every staff member will be treated fairly
Owning a mistake of his own openly and explaining the fix
Visiting the head office more often than the rural offices
Giving staff a day off after the first month of his term
questions.why: People watch what leaders do. Owning a mistake openly shows accountability and makes it safer for staff to do the same.

questions.q: What percentage of annual targets did the registry meet, and what is the response rate to the survey?
questions.why: 22 ÷ 40 × 100 = 55%. 375 ÷ 500 × 100 = 75%. The 60% is the share of replies that knew the plan, not the response rate.

questions.q: How should Mrs Reid use the result that only 55% of annual targets were met?
o: Publish a scorecard, have unit heads explain misses and agree fixes
Keep the result within the board, to avoid discouraging the staff
Lower next year's targets to match the level reached this year
Blame the two units with the lowest results in her next report
questions.why: A result is useful when it is shared and acted on. A scorecard, explanations from unit heads and agreed recovery actions turn the figures into improvement.

questions.q: Which unit plan is best aligned to the corporate plan's aim to halve complaint response times?
o: The registry will hold a staff sports day in the first quarter of next year
The records unit will buy new filing cabinets for all of its offices
The finance unit will reduce stationery costs by 10% across the year
The complaints unit will answer 90% of complaints in five working days
questions.why: An aligned unit plan has a clear link, a measure and a date. The other plans may be good ideas but do not serve the plan's aim.

questions.q: In the survey, only 60% of those who replied knew what the plan was trying to achieve. What does this show?
o: The survey was badly designed and its results should be ignored
The staff are not interested in what the organisation is trying to do
The plan has not been well communicated, so communication must improve
The CEO should repeat the survey until the figure is much higher
questions.why: If four in ten staff do not know the plan's aim, they cannot work towards it. The result is a prompt for better communication in every unit.

questions.q: What is the best way for Mrs Francis to gain the support of the other directors for a shared database?
o: Tell them the Permanent Secretary wants it, to save time
Build the database first and then ask each director to use it
Learn each director's concerns and show how it helps their division
Ask the board to order the divisions to hand over their data
questions.why: Influence without authority begins with listening and showing a benefit for each person. Orders or surprises tend to produce resistance.

questions.q: What best describes 'working in silos' in this ministry?
o: The ministry has too few staff for the work it must do
Each division works alone and shares little with the other
The divisions have the same targets and the same data
Staff in the ministry do not use computers
questions.why: Silos are units that work alone, so advice conflicts and work is repeated or wasted.

questions.q: Farmers receive contradictory advice and produce is wasted. What is the best action for the senior leadership?
o: Map the farmer's journey together and agree joint fixes
Merge the divisions by order, without consulting the staff
Ask each division to write a report showing why the other is at fault
Tell farmers to contact only the marketing division from now on
questions.why: The problem lies between the divisions. Mapping the whole journey from the farmer's point of view, with shared targets, fixes it jointly and gives both sides a stake.

questions.q: Which step best fits the CEO's wish that all 600 staff hear the news on the same day?
o: A letter posted to each office, to arrive within the week
A briefing for the senior team alone, who will pass it on when they can
An email to the board, which will then tell the staff itself
An all-staff briefing, then team briefings by managers that day
questions.why: A single message from the top makes sure everyone hears the same thing, and same-day team briefings answer questions and give local detail.

questions.q: Rumours say that 40 payroll clerks will lose their jobs, and no decision has been made. What should Mr Gray say?
o: That the rumours are false and no one will ever lose a job
Nothing, until all the decisions have been made
That the clerks should look for other jobs to be safe
What is known and not known, and when staff will hear more
questions.why: Honest information about what is and is not decided, with a date for the next update, prevents rumours from filling the gap without promising what cannot be guaranteed.

questions.q: The first office completes its move to the central payroll unit smoothly, and Mr Gray announces the results to all staff. Which Kotter step is this?
o: Creating a sense of urgency
Building a guiding coalition
Generating short-term wins
Anchoring the change in the culture
questions.why: Showing early, visible results builds credibility and momentum. It is the sixth of Kotter's steps; anchoring comes last, once the change is established.

questions.q: The adviser asks Dr Morgan to delay publication of an audit report. What is the best response?
o: Delay it for a week, to allow the new Minister time to settle in
Say publication follows the law, record the request and inform her superior
Publish it at once, without telling the Minister's office or the board
Ask the director of audit to remove the criticism from the report
questions.why: A senior public servant is politically neutral and follows the law and procedure. She declines politely, records the request and informs her superior.

questions.q: One director has accepted a free weekend at a resort from a bidding firm. What should Dr Morgan do?
o: Take the director off the contract decision and apply the code
Say nothing, since the weekend is over and nothing can be undone
Ask the firm to give the same gift to every director, to be fair to all
Wait until the contract is awarded and then look into the whole matter
questions.why: Hospitality from a bidder creates a conflict and a perception of favour. The director should step back from the decision, and the matter should be handled under the code of conduct.

questions.q: The new Minister decides on a policy that differs from the previous government's. How should Dr Morgan, as permanent secretary, respond?
o: Give frank advice on options and risks, then carry out the lawful decision
Refuse to act until the decision is made by the board of the ministry
Delay the work in the hope that the policy will be changed again
Carry out the decision without giving any advice, to stay neutral
questions.why: Neutrality does not mean silence. A senior public servant advises honestly, then implements lawful decisions of the government of the day.

questions.q: What was the completion rate, and what was the cost per participant?
questions.why: 12 ÷ 15 × 100 = 80%. 3,000,000 ÷ 15 = 200,000. The cost per participant uses all 15 who started.

questions.q: By how many percentage points did the share of staff reporting useful feedback rise?
o: 68 points
30.8 points
16 points
52 points
questions.why: 68 - 52 = 16 percentage points. A percentage change would be 16 ÷ 52 = about 30.8%, which is a different measure.

questions.q: Which feature of the programme is most likely to build strong leaders?
o: A single three-day residential course at the start of the year
Coaching, stretch assignments, learning sets and feedback together
A reading list of leadership books sent to each manager by email
A written test of leadership theory at the end of the year
questions.why: Leadership grows through practice, coaching and feedback. A mix of methods works better than a one-off course or reading alone.
